summary: Kole Jain walks through 20 web design resources he considers underrated for 2025, most of them free or mostly free. They cover ready-made UI elements (Uiverse, the Relume Figma kit), logos (Logo System, Logoipsum), animation (Phase), font pairing and display fonts (Fontjoy and a small display-font site), inspiration galleries (trending.design, Design Spells for micro-interactions, Unsectioned for page sections), imagery (Burst stock photos, Durves, Endless Tools 3D, Isocons isometric icons, Photo Gradient mesh gradients, Handy Arrows) and learning or career sources (UX of AI, Design Sphere podcasts, Wall of Portfolios). The video teaches no design method; its value for a design system is a list of where to find inspiration, placeholders and assets, plus a few stated reasons, such as beginners pairing fonts badly, Figma falling short for mesh gradients and for drawing arrows, and layout variety mattering. The picks are the presenter's opinions from January 2025, so availability and pricing may have changed.
key_ideas: Uiverse offers buttons, animations and elements that can be pasted straight into Figma with a Copy to Figma button, which helps when a Figma file is still empty.
Beginner designers tend to pair fonts badly, so a generator like Fontjoy can suggest a pairing with one button.
Phase is presented as an easier way to animate Figma designs than Figma plugins or After Effects, with an editor very similar to Figma.
Figma cannot produce everything a dedicated mesh-gradient tool like Photo Gradient can, so the source suggests using such a tool instead of switching to Photoshop.
Variety in layout matters, and Unsectioned makes it easier by splitting real websites into searchable sections.
Micro-interactions are a niche subject, so Design Spells curates the best ones from a ton of brands, including million- and billion-dollar companies.
Logo libraries (Logo System, Logoipsum) help designers who are weak at logos, giving them many logos to scroll through.
Burst, Shopify's free stock photo site, is smaller than Pexels but probably better organized, and the source argues you can never have too many stock photo sources.
Isocons offers isometric icons that can be switched between rounded and sharp and given a thicker or thinner stroke.
Relume's Figma kit is a very large community file (about 54 pages) that can be found in Figma without signing up to Relume.
Figma's pencil tool is limited for arrows, so a dedicated arrow library such as Handy Arrows gives more variety.
Seeing a designer's experience and location next to their portfolio (Wall of Portfolios) puts the work in perspective and discourages unfair self-comparison.
Because most designers will eventually work with or near AI, studying UX of AI helps build a feel for it.
3D is often called the next big thing, and Endless Tools offers customizable 3D resources in case it is, though some are limited.
Display fonts are something the presenter is always short of, which makes a small display-font site one of his favorite resources on the list.

rules.rule: If you struggle to pair fonts, let a font-pairing tool such as Fontjoy suggest a custom pairing.
rules.why: Beginner designers are pretty awful at pairing fonts; Fontjoy maps fonts on a 3D plane and returns a custom pairing with one button.
rules.evidence: beginner designers are pretty awful when it comes to pairing fonts together

rules.rule: Make mesh gradients in a dedicated gradient tool such as Photo Gradient rather than in Figma.
rules.why: You couldn't do all of this in Figma; the alternative is switching to Photoshop, and a dedicated tool keeps it simple with presets and settings.
rules.evidence: you definitely couldn't do all of this in figma

rules.rule: Animate Figma designs in Phase instead of Figma animation plugins or After Effects.
rules.why: Its editor is very similar to Figma, and the presenter found it much easier to use than After Effects and better than earlier plugins.
rules.evidence: it's way easier to do it on this platform

rules.rule: When looking for a page layout, search real website sections (for example on Unsectioned) to get variety.
rules.why: Variety in a layout is everything, but the right one can be hard to find.
rules.evidence: Variety in a layout is everything

rules.rule: Use a curated collection of micro-interactions from established brands, such as Design Spells, as a reference.
rules.why: Micro-interactions are a niche subject, and million- and billion-dollar companies come up with inventive ones.
rules.evidence: curated all of the best micro interactions

rules.rule: Start an empty Figma file from ready-made buttons, animations and elements, such as Uiverse items pasted with Copy to Figma.
rules.why: It helps when your Figma file looks like a big gray abyss, and you don't need to read the code.
rules.evidence: your figma files looking like a big gray Abyss

rules.rule: Use a dedicated arrow library such as Handy Arrows instead of drawing arrows with Figma's pencil tool.
rules.why: Figma's pencil tool only gets you so far, and Handy Arrows has serious variety.
rules.evidence: figma's pencil tool really only gets you so far

rules.rule: Keep more than one stock photo source, for example Burst alongside Pexels or Pixabay.
rules.why: Burst is smaller than Pexels but better organized, and the presenter says you can never have too many stock photo websites.
rules.evidence: you can never have too many stock photo websites

rules.rule: When comparing your portfolio with showcased ones, take each designer's experience and background into account (Wall of Portfolios lists them).
rules.why: It puts their portfolio in perspective so you compare yourself less to professionals with many years of experience.
rules.evidence: they break down the experience of the designer

rules.rule: Build a feel for AI user experience (for example through UX of AI) before designing AI features.
rules.why: Most designers will at some point design with AI or in AI-adjacent fields, and AI can be as stupid as it is smart.
rules.evidence: AI can be as smart as it is stupid

rules.rule: If you are weak at logos, browse a logo library such as Logo System or Logoipsum for ideas.
rules.why: The presenter says he is bad at designing logos, and these libraries give him plenty of logos to scroll through and borrow from.
rules.evidence: great website if you suck at logos

rules.rule: For isometric icons, use a customizable set such as Isocons and choose rounded or sharp corners and the stroke weight.
rules.why: Isocons has a ton of isometric icons, all customizable, and gathers the ones you add in a folder where you can see and customize them together.
rules.evidence: you can change if they're rounded or sharp and how fat the stroke is

rules.rule: For a large base of sections, layouts and elements in Figma, use the Relume Figma kit from the Figma Community; no Relume sign-up is needed.
rules.why: The kit is massive, about 54 pages of sections, layouts and elements, and it is a Figma community file.
rules.evidence: search for it on figma without even needing to sign up

rules.rule: If you want 3D in a design, start from customizable 3D resources such as Endless Tools.
rules.why: Many people say 3D will be the next big thing; Endless Tools has quirky 3D resources you can customize yourself, though some are limited and more are being added.
rules.evidence: 3D is going to be the next big thing

rules.rule: For a crypto or modern SaaS landing page, consider a slider-driven tool such as Durves.
rules.why: The presenter calls it a niche tool but could see himself using it for a crypto or modern software-as-a-service landing page.
rules.evidence: crypto or modern software as a service landing page

rules.rule: Keep a curated source of display fonts, such as the small display-font site the presenter ranks among his favorites (captioned 'typ faces. today').
rules.why: He is chronically in need of better display fonts, and the site has some really cool ones, though not many.
rules.evidence: chronically in need of better display fonts

caveats: A list of tools and sites, not design guidance; the rules here are the presenter's tool preferences, not tested practice.
Dated January 2025; the sites, their features and whether they are free ('totally or at least mostly free') may have changed.
Self-promotion: the description promotes the presenter's web design challenge with a $2,000 prize pool, and the ending promotes his design community of over 13,000 designers.

Several names are auto-caption mis-hearings: 'UI verse' is Uiverse, 'fonty' is Fontjoy and 'derves' is Durves (confirmed by the description links); 'reloom' is Relume, 'ISO cons' is Isocons and 'pixels' is Pexels [inferred].

The description's timestamp list is cut off after 4:23, and the names of item 11 (a playlist site, credited in the captions to 'L files') and item 12 (a display-font site captioned 'typ faces. today') are unclear.
The captions also mention 'logo.com' as an extra logo resource right after Logoipsum; it is not in the numbered list.
The presenter jokes about stealing logos from Logoipsum; check each resource's license before using its assets in a real product [inferred].
